top.line: Open source is a copyright licence, not a free-for-all
top.para: Common misconceptions are corrected: a few maintainers control what goes in, most projects are run by a handful of people, security depends on paid review time, somebody always pays, open weights are a compiled binary, and no licence means all rights reserved. The real power of open source is that nobody can lock you in.

in-short.line: Open source is licensed control, with no lock-in
in-short.para: An open source licence uses copyright to grant copying, use and change; it began as the GPL's copyleft, reframed as open source in 1998. Maintainers control what goes in, security depends on review time and money, and somebody always pays. The point is the freedom to read, run, fix and move software.

history.line: From GPL copyleft to open source, still a licence
history.para: Stallman's GPL, first released in 1989, made sharing a condition, and Christine Peterson proposed open source in February 1998 as Perens and Raymond founded the OSI. Linux adopted GPL version 2 in 1992 and stayed. Apache 2.0 adds a patent grant, and having no licence means all rights reserved.

control.line: A few maintainers decide; the control is simply visible
control.para: Serious projects have one or a handful of maintainers who review, test, sign off and often refuse contributions, recording provenance through certificates or contributor agreements. Anybody can fork and change their own copy, but nobody can change yours without you. Visible control is a strength.

contribute.line: Most open source projects are run by few people
contribute.para: The barrier to contributing is lower than for proprietary software, which often cannot even be built. But apart from a very small minority of very popular projects, most are run by a small number of people. Expecting a large community leads people to miss what is actually there.

security.line: Security depends on paid review time, not on openness
security.para: Open source is neither much more nor less secure than proprietary software. What matters is whether someone had the time, usually paid, to review and test it, and how widely it is used. Black Duck finds open source in almost all commercial codebases, so closing a product only hides its dependencies.

cost.line: Open source is not free: somebody is always paying
cost.para: Tidelift's 2024 survey found around 60% of maintainers call themselves unpaid hobbyists, and paid ones follow more security practices. The xz utils backdoor of March 2024 hit a library maintained by one person with no time or money. Maintainers should be paid, and agents may finally make the workflows practical.

weights.line: Open weights are a compiled binary, not open source
weights.para: Weights can be run and fine-tuned but not rebuilt, so labs are right to say open weights. The OSI's Open Source AI Definition requires training code, parameters and enough data information to build an equivalent system. Open weights remain a large economic advantage, just a different thing.

fud.line: What matters is how a tool is used
fud.para: Fear about open-weight models echoes past worries; Metasploit made exploitation easier and the world adjusted. Some highly destructive capabilities should not be released, and some technology will be controlled. Hosting and distribution are themselves points of control, so open source is never a free-for-all.

power.line: The power of open source is freedom from lock-in
power.para: Not contributions but the ability to read, run, fix and move software, even if its company is sold or disappears, plus the whole development workflow with history, tests and builds. That is why there is no sovereignty without it. open-source.sgit.ai's first lesson: open source is not free.

limits.line: Not legal advice; history shortened; figures are surveys
limits.para: Licences are legal instruments, so read them and ask a lawyer. Earlier permissive licences existed alongside the GPL, with the fuller story on open-source.sgit.ai. Tidelift's 60% is self-description, and contributions do happen; the claim is only that they are not the point or the norm.

sources.line: Sources: OSI, choosealicense, Black Duck, Tidelift and Wikipedia
sources.para: A voice memo of 12 October 2026, with history corrected from sources. The Open Source Initiative and open-source.sgit.ai's timeline, choosealicense.com, Black Duck's OSSRA, Tidelift's 2024 maintainer report via The Register, the Open Source AI Definition, and Wikipedia on the xz case.
